primary_meaning: In most Christian teaching, barley symbolizes humble, lowly provision — the bread of the poor — through which God works and provides. Because barley was the cheaper grain eaten by the poor (about half the value of wheat), it is read as a picture of humility, lowliness, and God's use of small or despised means, most famously in the boy's five barley loaves with which Jesus feeds the five thousand. Closely intertwined with this is a second widely taught meaning: barley as the firstfruits grain of the early (Passover-season) harvest, and therefore a type of resurrection and of the 'firstfruits' people of God.
primary_basis: John 6:9-13 (the five barley loaves in the feeding of the five thousand)
Judges 7:13 (the barley loaf tumbling into the Midianite camp, representing lowly Gideon/Israel)
Ruth 1:22; 2:17, 23 (Ruth gleaning in the barley harvest; the poor gleaner motif)
Revelation 6:6 (barley priced at a third of wheat, marking it as the cheap grain of the poor)
Exodus 9:31-32 (barley already in the ear at the plague of hail, establishing it as the early grain)
Leviticus 23:10-11 and Deuteronomy 16:9 (the firstfruits sheaf of the early harvest, traditionally understood as barley, waved at Passover season)
1 Corinthians 15:20-23 (Christ as 'firstfruits,' linked typologically to the barley firstfruits offering)

alternatives.meaning: Firstfruits / resurrection typology: barley, as the first grain ripe at Passover, prefigures Christ's resurrection as the 'firstfruits' and, in some prophetic-typology teaching, a 'first harvest' company of believers (with wheat as a later harvest at Pentecost). Especially prominent in Messianic, dispensational, and popular prophecy teaching.
basis: John 20 read against the Feast of Firstfruits

alternatives.meaning: Patristic/medieval allegory: the barley loaves in John 6 represent the Old Testament Law or the letter of Scripture — nourishing but encased in a rough husk that must be broken open to reach the inner meaning (Augustine, Bede, and later allegorical commentators).
basis: John 6:9 as expounded in Augustine's Tractates on the Gospel of John and Bede's homilies

alternatives.meaning: Scarcity, judgment, and cheapness: barley as a marker of famine pricing and divine judgment, or of low valuation (the price of a slave-wife, an adulteress, or false prophecy).
basis: Numbers 5:15 (the barley jealousy offering without oil or frankincense)

alternatives.meaning: Simple agricultural/literal reading: barley carries no fixed symbolic meaning and functions simply as a seasonal and economic detail (dating events to spring, signaling poverty or ordinary agrarian life).
basis: Exodus 9:31-32 read in mainstream critical and historical commentaries

notes: Barley has a recognizable cluster of associations rather than one settled symbolic meaning. The two most repeated interpretive threads are (1) humility/poor man's bread and (2) Passover-season firstfruits pointing to resurrection, and many teachers combine the two (the lowly grain that is nonetheless first to be raised/harvested). Academic biblical scholarship generally treats barley non-symbolically as an economic and calendrical marker, while devotional, typological, and prophecy-oriented literature supplies the symbolic readings. Because prominence differs sharply between popular typology teaching and mainstream commentary, no single interpretation can be called a settled consensus, though the humility/firstfruits pairing is the most widely recognizable.
